1.pericope_label: Now when he had ended all his sayings in the audience of the people, he entered into Capernaum. And a certain centurion’s servant, who was dear unto him, was sick, and ready to die. And when he heard of Jesus, he sent unto him the elders of the Jews, beseeching him that he would come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this: For he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue. Then Jesus went with them. And when he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying unto him, Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof: Wherefore neither thought I myself worthy to come unto thee: but say in a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man set under authority, having under me soldiers, and I say unto one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it. When Jesus heard these things, he marvelled at him, and turned him about, and said unto the people that followed him, I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. And they that were sent, returning to the house, found the servant whole that had been sick.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers Luke to Matthew on the two embassies, holding that the precision of his account leads us to receive it as the more accurate record and that it is also more true to nature, since the centurion was not likely to leave a slave so precious to him when he seemed in the agonies of death; he then turns the argument against himself, noting that Luke is here less precise than Matthew, who states the slave was sick of the palsy, and asking whether the physician had been unable to satisfy himself as to the nature of the disease. He reads the elders as elders without the article, the word rendered dear as precious, and the synagogue strictly as a known and conspicuous building. Robertson supplies the military frame, that a centurion commanded between fifty and a hundred men, with six centuries to a cohort and ten cohorts to a legion, and that the centurions named in the New Testament all seem to be fine men since Polybius states the best men held that position; he also holds the opening verse really belongs as the conclusion of the previous chapter, and reports Plummer's judgment that Matthew puts the message of both embassies into the centurion's own mouth.

Henry disposes of the discrepancy with Matthew by the maxim that what we do by another we are judged to do ourselves, so that the centurion did by his proxies what a man does by his attorney in taking possession, and thinks it probable he came himself at last; he also observes that Christ left it to his own works to praise him in the gates.

Chrysostom fastens on the form of the request, that the centurion held a right opinion of the Lord since he said not pray but command, and that lest the Lord should from humility refuse him he added that he too was a man set under authority.

Bede explains the pattern of the two accounts from Luke's habit, which is to abridge or purposely pass by whatever he sees plainly set forth by the other Evangelists and to explain more carefully what they omit; he draws out the centurion's inference, that if a man subject to a tribune can command his inferiors, much more can he who is God fulfil whatever he wishes, not by the presence of his body only but by the services of his angels, and he narrows the commendation to the men of the present age rather than the patriarchs and prophets, because they were instructed in the precepts of the Law and the Prophets while the centurion, with no one to teach him, believed of his own accord. Ambrose finds the Greek sharper than the English, since read as not even in Israel this faith is preferred even to that of the more elect who see God, and closes on the servant, that a master's good deed may advantage his servants not only through the merit of faith but through the practice of discipline.

debates: Why Matthew has the centurion come in person while Luke has him send twice, where Henry answers with the maxim that what we do by another we do ourselves, Robertson that Luke gives the details and Matthew a summary, Ellicott that Luke is simply the more accurate and more natural record, and Bede that Luke habitually explains what the others pass over.
Whether Luke is in fact the more precise Evangelist here, which Ellicott asserts on the embassies and then doubts on the disease, since Matthew names the palsy and Luke does not.
Where the opening verse belongs, which Robertson holds really concludes the previous chapter rather than beginning this one.
outliers: Ellicott identifies the synagogue the centurion built with ruins lately discovered at Capernaum, reading the article strictly as a well-known and conspicuous building and probably the only one there.
Robertson notes that the centurion built the synagogue all by himself and at his own expense.

11.pericope_label: And it came to pass the day after, that he went into a city called Nain; and many of his disciples went with him, and much people. Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow: and much people of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not. And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother. And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people. And this rumour of him went forth throughout all Judea, and throughout all the region round about. And the disciples of John shewed him of all these things.

schools.summary: Ellicott builds a case for the source of this narrative, which is Luke's alone: the name survives with hardly any alteration in the modern Nein on the north-western edge of the Little Hermon, the approach is a steep ascent and the rock on either side is full of sepulchral caves, and from the circumstances he infers that the miracle fixed itself in the memories of the devout women named in the next chapter and that Luke had it from them, an inference he supports from the absolute use of the term the Lord, one of the few places where it stands instead of the name. He supplies what was touched, not a closed coffin like the mummy cases of Egypt but an open bier with the corpse in its winding sheet and a napkin laid over the face, and observes that the bearers must have marvelled that a known Teacher should touch what most Rabbis would have avoided as pollution.

Henry works on the attestation rather than the source, noting that the miracle was done in sight of two crowds meeting at the gate, one of disciples following Jesus and one of relations and neighbours following the bier, so that there was a sufficient number to attest it, and reckoning the raising a greater proof of divine authority than the healings since by no power of nature can the dead be raised; on the grief he observes that the mother had depended on her son as the staff of her old age and he proved a broken reed, as every man at his best estate is, that being a widow she was broken with breach upon breach, and that the young man was cut off in the beginning of his days since man comes forth like a flower and is cut down.

Titus anticipates the objection that the centurion's servant was not going to die, and says the Evangelist forestalls it by making plain that this young man was already dead; he then measures the act against its precedents and finds none of them adequate, the Saviour being unlike Elijah mourning over the son of the widow of Sarepta, unlike Elisha who laid his own body upon the body of the dead, and unlike Peter who prayed for Tabitha, but none other than he who calls those things which be not as though they were.

Cyril fastens on the touch, that the miracle was performed not only in word but by touching the bier so that we might know the body of Christ is powerful to save, and that as iron applied to fire does the work of fire, so the flesh united to the Word becomes itself quickening and the banisher of death.

Bede fixes Nain as a city of Galilee within two miles of Mount Tabor and glosses the command not to weep as meaning cease to weep for one as dead whom you shall soon see rise again alive; he also observes that by the divine counsel large multitudes were accompanying the Lord, so that there might be many witnesses of so great a miracle.

debates: Where Luke got a narrative no other Gospel records, which Ellicott traces to the devout women of the following chapter on the evidence of the topography and of the absolute use of the term the Lord.
Whether the raising is a greater proof than the healings, which Henry affirms on the ground that no power of nature can raise the dead.

How the act stands to its Old Testament precedents, where Titus finds none of them adequate, neither Elijah nor Elisha nor Peter, since this is he who calls those things which be not as though they were.
outliers: Bede glosses the command not to weep as meaning cease to weep for one as dead whom you shall soon see rise again alive.
Ellicott reads the giving back of the son as the mother receiving him God-given in a higher sense than when she first rejoiced that a man-child was born.

19.pericope_label: And John calling unto him two of his disciples sent them to Jesus, saying, Art thou he that should come? or look we for another? When the men were come unto him, they said, John Baptist hath sent us unto thee, saying, Art thou he that should come? or look we for another? And in that same hour he cured many of their infirmities and plagues, and of evil spirits; and unto many that were blind he gave sight. Then Jesus answering said unto them, Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached. And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me. And when the messengers of John were departed, he began to speak unto the people concerning John, What went ye out into the wilderness for to see? A reed shaken with the wind? But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings’ courts. But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and much more than a prophet. This is he, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee. For I say unto you, Among those that are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist: but he that is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. And all the people that heard him, and the publicans, justified God, being baptized with the baptism of John. But the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, being not baptized of him. And the Lord said, Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation? and to what are they like? They are like unto children sitting in the marketplace, and calling one to another, and saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned to you, and ye have not wept. For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine; and ye say, He hath a devil. The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners! But wisdom is justified of all her children.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Luke alone gives the number of disciples sent and that the best manuscripts have them sent to the Lord, and that the statement of cures wrought in that same hour is peculiar to Luke and adds much force, since Christ pointed to what was passing before the questioners' eyes; he finds Luke's gorgeously apparelled more vivid than Matthew's soft clothing, bringing out ostentatious display and effeminate self-indulgence common in the house of Herod, and traces a touch of brutal vindictiveness in the bright robe those same Herodians afterwards put upon the Prophet of Nazareth. On the two classes he thinks the statement interposed for Gentile readers and would render the clauses acknowledged God as righteous and, against the unhappy ambiguity of the English, frustrated for themselves the counsel of God; he places the two classes at opposite extremes of the nation's social and religious life.

Calvin takes the two classes Matthew omits and makes them the hinge, since the passage throws no small light on the connection and the obstinacy of the scribes in despising God gave rise to the expostulation; he reads the Lord as intending from the beginning to hold out this example, that neither that age nor posterity might judge the Gospel by the approbation of men. On the children's song he is sharpest, holding that Christ borrowed from children the materials of his reproof so that nothing more was needed to condemn the scribes, however distinguished, than a song children sang in the market-place; John sang a plaintive song and the Lord a cheerful one and neither succeeded; and against those who place the highest perfection in outward austerity he observes that on that principle John would rank higher than the Son of God.

Henry explains the Baptist's message from the circumstances rather than from any failure of faith, putting the need for confirmation on John's disciples as much as on John: Christ had not yet publicly declared himself and would not have those who knew him speak of it until the proofs were completed in his resurrection, the great men of the Jewish church had not owned him, and nothing of the expected Messianic grandeur was to be seen about him; Christ therefore left it to his own works to praise him in the gates.

Titus argues from the geography, that they left their cities for a desert where there is no pleasantness and can only have done it out of care for this man, and is precise on the title of messenger, that John is called an angel not by nature, being by nature a man, but because he exercised the office in heralding the advent.

Cyril sees the Lord forestalling a harsher inference, that if John were ignorant of Jesus until now his earlier pointing him out as the Lamb of God was worthless, and places the discourse so as to quench that feeling before it could do injury; he glosses the reed as a rebuke to the crowd's own suspicion, since they crossed long journeys into the desert in vain if they now think him so fickle as to bend whichever way the wind moves, which is how a man appears who lightly avows ignorance of what he knows.

Ambrose praises the character rather than the office, that John preferred the way of righteousness to the love of life and swerved not through fear of death, and turns the reed into an allegory of the world as a desert where men puffed up with a fleshly mind and vaunting themselves in frail glory are tossed about by a restless life; greater than a prophet, he says, was he in whom the prophets terminate, for many desired to see him whom John saw and baptized.

debates: Why the Baptist sent at all, which Henry explains from the circumstances of a Messiah not yet publicly declared and without worldly grandeur, and which Cyril reads as the occasion for the Lord to forestall the inference that John's earlier testimony was worthless.

What the reed means, where Cyril makes it a rebuke to the crowd's suspicion of fickleness in John, Ambrose an allegory of worldly men tossed by a restless life, and Titus an argument from the barrenness of the desert they crossed to reach him.
What the two classes of hearers are doing in the narrative, which Calvin makes the hinge of the whole expostulation and Ellicott takes for a statement interposed for Gentile readers.
outliers: Calvin holds that Christ deliberately borrowed the materials of his reproof from a song children sang in the market-place, so that nothing more was needed to condemn the scribes however distinguished they were.
Calvin observes that if the highest perfection consisted in outward austerity of life, then on that principle John would rank higher than the Son of God.

36.pericope_label: And one of the Pharisees desired him that he would eat with him. And he went into the Pharisee’s house, and sat down to meat. And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster box of ointment, And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. Now when the Pharisee which had bidden him saw it, he spake within himself, saying, This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner. And Jesus answering said unto him, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And he saith, Master, say on. There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty. And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most? Simon answered and said, I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most. And he said unto him, Thou hast rightly judged. And he turned to the woman, and said unto Simon, Seest thou this woman? I entered into thine house, thou gavest me no water for my feet: but she hath washed my feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head. Thou gavest me no kiss: but this woman since the time I came in hath not ceased to kiss my feet. My head with oil thou didst not anoint: but this woman hath anointed my feet with ointment. Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven. And they that sat at meat with him began to say within themselves, Who is this that forgiveth sins also? And he said to the woman, Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.

schools.summary: Ellicott refuses the identification of the woman outright: the widespread belief that she was Mary Magdalene has absolutely not a single jot or tittle of evidence in Scripture nor anything like a tradition in its favour, the earliest Fathers are silent, it was discussed and rejected early, and Ambrose and Augustine are doubtful, and it first gained acceptance through the authority of Gregory and the choice of this narrative for her feast. He reconstructs the slight in the invitation, which had no real respect in it and was hardly more than ostentatious patronage, since the courtesies due to well-nigh every guest were in Simon's judgment superfluous; and on the parable he grants that the words admit two interpretations equally tenable but holds the whole drift in favour of love as the consequence of forgiveness rather than its ground, noting that the later absolution did not convey forgiveness for the first time but came to banish every lingering doubt.

Calvin holds the parable's whole scope is to show Simon wrong in condemning a woman whom the heavenly judge acquits, and will not let love be the price: the argument is taken not from the cause but from the effect, since until a favour has been received it cannot awaken gratitude, and the cause of reciprocal love is declared to be a free forgiveness; he calls it a gross blunder that most commentators have made the woman earn her pardon, and finds the exposure of Simon's silent thought meant to assure us all that no sinner need fear rejection by one who invites with outstretched arms.

Henry reaches the same verdict on the woman's identity by another argument, that the identification is commonly made but he finds no ground in Scripture for it, and that the Magdalene is described elsewhere as one out of whom seven devils were cast, which is not mentioned here; he notes that the Pharisee did not believe in Christ since he will not own him a prophet, and that Christ accepted the invitation anyway, taking the same liberty with Pharisees as with publicans in hopes of doing them good.

Ambrose keeps the question of how this anointing stands to Matthew's, observing that Matthew has the ointment poured on the head and was therefore unwilling to call the woman a sinner while here the sinner anoints the feet, so that she cannot be the same lest the Evangelists seem at variance, though he allows the difficulty may also be solved by a difference of merit and of time. Augustine resolves it the other way, that the same Mary did this twice, once as Luke relates and again at Bethany in the occurrence the other three record. Gregory the Great reads the ointment as the sweet savour of a good report, so that good works sprinkle the Church with it.

debates: Who the woman was, where Ellicott and Henry independently reject the Magdalene identification for want of any scriptural ground, Ellicott adding that it first gained acceptance through the authority of Gregory the Great.

Whether this anointing and the one at Bethany are the same event, which Ambrose denies on the ground that Matthew anoints the head and declines to call the woman a sinner, and which Augustine affirms by having the same Mary do it twice.

Whether the woman's love is the ground of her forgiveness or its consequence, where Calvin and Ellicott agree on the consequence from opposite starting points, Calvin from cause and effect and Ellicott from the drift of the parable, Calvin calling the other reading a gross blunder of most commentators.
outliers: Ellicott fills in each omitted courtesy, the kiss that became the kiss of peace in the Liturgies and the anointing of the head that brought comfort to one who had journeyed under the burning sun of Syria, and marks the contrast between olive oil and the costlier ointment.

Ellicott observes that Simon, like the woman of Samaria, located the prophetic character not in prediction but in the power to read the secrets of men's hearts, and detects a tone of satisfaction at having caught out an inconsistency.
